title: Jewellery for a simple kurti: everyday ethnic looks
description: Five easy jewellery looks for a plain kurti, for college, office, errands, evenings and temple visits, plus which pieces survive daily wear best.
keywords: how to style a plain kurti
intro: A plain kurti needs only two or three pieces to look finished: one focus piece near the face, one small detail at the wrist, and nothing that fights the neckline. Earrings usually do the most work. Below are five everyday looks you can copy, and a note on which jewellery holds up to daily use.

sections.heading: Start with the neckline
paragraphs: Before reaching for jewellery, look at the kurti's neck. It tells you whether to wear a necklace at all.

Length matters too. With a short kurti over jeans, a mid-length pendant ending at the chest looks balanced. With a long Anarkali-style kurti, the eye travels down the whole outfit, so longer earrings and a slightly longer chain feel more in proportion.
list: Round neck: a short pendant sitting just below the collarbone, or earrings alone
V neck: a pendant on a thin chain that echoes the V shape
Mandarin or band collar: no necklace; let jhumkas or studs carry the look
Keyhole or embroidered yoke: the neck is already decorated, so stick to studs

sections.heading: Look 1: college or a casual day out
paragraphs: Pair a cotton kurti and jeans with medium oxidised or Meenakari jhumkas and a thread bracelet or a few thin bangles. Skip the necklace. This is the most forgiving look there is, and jhumkas instantly make even a printed kurti look intentional.
If you carry a sling bag or backpack, avoid long necklaces, which tangle with straps.
For printed kurtis, pick out the least obvious colour in the print and repeat it in your earrings. It looks far more thought-through than matching the main colour.

sections.heading: Look 2: office
paragraphs: Small Kundan studs or a pair of simple drops, a slim watch, and optionally a short pendant. A [925 sterling silver pendant](/silver) on a fine chain is ideal for workdays, because it looks polished with both ethnic and western clothes and does not jangle on a keyboard.
Choose one metal tone and stay with it across earrings, pendant and watch for a neat finish.

If your office is formal, keep earrings no longer than the earlobe plus a centimetre or two. On Fridays or festival days at work, a pair of small Kundan jhumkas adds a festive touch without looking out of place in a meeting.

sections.heading: Look 3: errands and market runs
paragraphs: Comfort comes first when you are carrying bags and moving in and out of autos. Studs, one bangle or kada, and that is it. Avoid anything that dangles and can catch on a dupatta or a shopping bag handle, and leave your favourite statement earrings at home on rainy days.
A long kurti with palazzos looks surprisingly put-together with just a pair of bold studs and a bindi.

sections.heading: Look 4: evening plans with friends or family
paragraphs: This is where you can turn the same kurti into something dressier. Swap the studs for chandbalis or statement jhumkas, add a stack of bangles on one hand and a ring on the other. If the kurti is solid-coloured, pick earrings with a coloured stone or Meenakari detail that contrasts with it, for example pink with a mint kurti or green with mustard.
Changing just the earrings and adding a bright dupatta is often enough to go from day to dinner.

sections.heading: Look 5: a temple visit or puja at home
paragraphs: Many people prefer to keep things simple and traditional here. A pair of small jhumkas, glass or metal bangles, and perhaps a rudraksha mala or a pendant with a deity motif. Our [Divine collection](/divine) has gold-plated rudraksha chains with Om, Trishul, Ganesha and Shiva pendants that sit well over a cotton or chikankari kurti. Customs differ between families and temples, so follow what feels right for you.

sections.heading: What survives daily wear
paragraphs: Everyday jewellery takes more wear than party jewellery: sweat, sanitiser, rain and the odd night you forget to take it off. Gold-plated, Kundan and oxidised pieces are made for occasional wear, so take them off before washing hands, applying lotion or sleeping, and wipe them with a soft dry cloth before putting them away in a zip pouch.

925 sterling silver is the better choice for something you wear daily. It can tarnish over time, especially in humid weather, but it can be cleaned with a silver polishing cloth and kept in an airtight bag. If the silver is gold-plated, polish gently so the plating is not rubbed off.
Keep your daily pieces in one small box near the mirror. When everything is in sight, you are far more likely to actually wear it.

faq.q: Which earrings look best with a kurti?
faq.a: Jhumkas are the most versatile. Studs suit office and collared kurtis, while chandbalis suit evening and festive kurtis.

faq.q: Should I wear a necklace with a kurti?
faq.a: Only if the neckline is plain and open. With collars, yokes or heavy embroidery, skip the necklace and focus on earrings.

faq.q: Can I wear a silver pendant with an ethnic kurti?
faq.a: Yes. A simple silver pendant looks clean with cotton and linen kurtis, especially if your earrings are also silver-tone.

faq.q: Is imitation jewellery okay for daily wear?
faq.a: Light pieces are fine for regular use if you keep them away from water, perfume and sweat. For true daily wear, 925 silver holds up better.
